newsitem.title: USA: Clinton orders troops to Gulf, defends Iraq policy.
newsitem.headline: Clinton orders troops to Gulf, defends Iraq policy.

text.p: President Bill Clinton ordered 3,500 U.S. troops to Kuwait on Tuesday as part of a plan to "keep Saddam Hussein in a box" while the Gulf crisis showed signs of easing, reducing chances of a clash with Iraq.

There was no letup in Republican sniping at Clinton's handling of events in the Gulf, however. "Saddam Hussein is far better off than he was two weeks ago," Sen. John McCain of Arizona said after Clinton reviewed the crisis with lawmakers.

McCain and other partisan critics contend the latest U.S. brush with Iraq, which included two U.S. cruise missile strikes and expansion of a no-fly zone in southern Iraq in retaliation for Iraqi attacks on minority Kurds, exposed a rift in the Gulf War alliance and permitted Iraqi President Saddam Hussein to regain control in the north of his country.

Speaking with reporters after a meeting with congressional leaders, Clinton disputed a Washington Post report that he was reconsidering reinforcing U.S. ground forces in Kuwait because tensions with Iraq were subsiding.

"I authorised the deployment last weekend and ... the deployment orders were signed last night," Clinton said in denying that plans to send the troops had been put on hold. "I was surprised when I read the story today (about possible suspension of the troop deployment), and I asked for an explanation of it, and none of our people had one ..."

Clinton did not say when the troops might actually go. They would join 1,500 U.S. soldiers already in Kuwait, one of the world's largest oil exporters, which was overrun by Iraqi troops in 1990. That invasion triggered the 1991 Gulf War.

At the Pentagon, an official said the deployment would occur in a matter of days. "The order has been received, and it will be 3,500 troops. I expect they will go in the coming days," the official, who asked not to be identified, said.
Clinton defended his ordering of cruise missile strikes against air defence facilities in southern Iraq two weeks ago in retaliation for an Iraqi move against Kurds in the north.

He said the attacks and expansion of a no-fly zone in southern Iraq from which Iraqi warplanes are excluded were designed to improve the U.S. strategic position in the area and "keep Saddam Hussein in a box and limit his ability to threaten his neighbours."

Defence Secretary William Perry, just back from a trip to the Middle East to rally support for the president's policy, said the Republican criticism of Clinton's performance in the election-year foreign policy test was unfounded.
"The bottom line ... is that the coalition is alive and well," Perry said at a news conference on his weekend visit to Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Bahrain, Turkey and Britain.

He at first said coalition leaders he conferred with in the Gulf and in Britain "offered support to Operation Southern Watch and said they will continue to support Operation Southern Watch in its expanded form." "Southern Watch" is the code name for allied air patrols to bar Iraqi warplanes from a no-fly zone covering southern Iraq.

Perry said the allies supported both a U.S. decision to expand the zone northward from the 32rd to the 33nd parallel and to increase the number of patrols. Later, however, he told reporters France did not support expansion of the zone.

Perry also said that after blindly launching six missiles at U.S. warplanes patrolling its airspace last week, Iraq had ceased its threatening military activity, reducing chances of another showdown with the United States. "In the last few days, the Iraqis have been backing off the threating moves they were making against our air crews. And, therefore, there is some reason for that hope," he said.

At the State Department, spokesman Nicholas Burns said the the United States had sent a fresh message to Iraq telling it not to interfere with Western enforcement of no-fly zones. He said the warning was faxed on Monday to the Iraqi mission at the United Nations in New York, the second such warning since the Iraq crisis erupted at the end of last month.

"The message that we conveyed to the Iraqis will remain in effect indefinitely. It has no expiration date. The United States will watch very closely to see whether Saddam Hussein backs up his words with actions," Burns said.
